title: What Is Spark-Gap Transmitter? — Definition
body:
Radio is wireless communication and broadcasting by electromagnetic waves: spark-gap and crystal sets, tube receivers (regenerative, TRF, superheterodyne), transistor portables, shortwave, ham radio, and CB. It carried the first wireless messages, the first mass broadcast medium, wartime traffic, and the transistor's first killer product.

In the context of this database, the Spark-Gap Transmitter is presented as one radio record among the radio history family. The original radio: high-voltage sparks radiating damped waves — broad, buzzy, and illegal by 1930.

title: Origins and History of Spark-Gap Transmitter
body:
The Spark-Gap Transmitter belongs to the 1890s–1920s era and traces to Marconi/Hertz lineage.

Hertz proved the waves (1887); Marconi wirelessed across the Atlantic (1901). Crystal sets with cat's-whisker detectors brought radio to hobbyists; Lee de Forest's Audion and Armstrong's regenerative (1912) and superheterodyne (1918) circuits made it practical. KDKA's 1920 election broadcast launched commercial radio; the 1920s–30s golden age filled parlors with cathedral cabinets. FM (Armstrong, 1933) fought AM interests for decades before winning on fidelity. WWII miniaturized radio for walkie-talkies and radar; the transistor (Regency TR-1, 1954; Sony TR-63, 1957) put radio in every pocket. Shortwave spanned the planet; ham radio built a global hobbyist network; CB (1970s) put truckers on channel 19.

Within that longer story, Spark-Gap Transmitter: Marconi's 1901 transatlantic used spark; the 'spark' is radio's first sound. Banned for interference; CW (continuous wave) replaced it.

title: How Spark-Gap Transmitter Works
body:
A transmitter varies (modulates) a carrier wave's amplitude (AM) or frequency (FM) with audio; the receiver's antenna picks up the carrier, a tuner selects its frequency, a detector strips the audio back off, and an amplifier drives the speaker. The superheterodyne converts every station to one fixed intermediate frequency (455 kHz AM, 10.7 MHz FM) where sharp filters and high gain are easy. Regenerative sets fed output back to the input for huge sensitivity from one tube. Crystal sets need no power at all — the galena junction rectifies the signal directly.

Applied to the Spark-Gap Transmitter (1890s–1920s, Marconi/Hertz lineage): Banned for interference; CW (continuous wave) replaced it.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Anatomy of Spark-Gap Transmitter — Components
body:
Every Spark-Gap Transmitter is an assembly of the radio history family's standard parts:

• Antenna — Captures RF: whip, loop, longwire, ferrite bar.
• Tuner — Variable capacitor/inductor selecting the station.
• Detector — Crystal, diode, or grid-leak: extracts audio from RF.
• IF strip — Fixed-frequency amplification and filtering (superhet).
• Local oscillator — Mixes with incoming RF to make the IF.
• Audio amplifier — From headphones to speaker power.
• Speaker — Electrodynamic cone; the radio's voice.
• Power supply — Batteries, AC transformer, or vibrator (car/farm sets).
• Tubes / transistors — The active devices doing the amplifying.
• Cabinet — Cathedral, tombstone, console — furniture as much as electronics.

When examining a surviving Spark-Gap Transmitter, identify these parts in order: Antenna, Tuner, Detector, IF strip, Local oscillator, Audio amplifier.

title: Radio History Glossary
body:
The working vocabulary of radio history:

• AM / FM — Amplitude vs frequency modulation; fidelity vs range trade.
• superheterodyne — Convert-to-IF architecture; Armstrong 1918, still universal.
• regenerative — Positive feedback for sensitivity; Armstrong 1912.
• TRF — Tuned Radio Frequency; amplification at the signal frequency.
• cat's whisker — Fine wire on galena crystal: the original semiconductor diode.
• coherer — Branly's metal-filings detector; Marconi's first receiver.
• selectivity / sensitivity — Separating stations vs hearing weak ones; the twin specs.
• IF — Intermediate frequency: 455 kHz AM, 10.7 MHz FM.
• shortwave — 3–30 MHz; bounces off the ionosphere worldwide.
• QSL card — Hobbyist confirmation of reception; a whole collecting world.
• DXing — Chasing distant stations; a sport with logs and awards.
• dead air — Silence on air; the broadcaster's nightmare.

title: Spark-Gap Transmitter in Culture
body:
Radio was the internet before the internet: families around the cathedral cabinet, FDR's fireside chats, WWII news from London, Wolfman Jack howling across the border at night. The transistor radio freed teenagers from the parlor — rock and roll in a shirt pocket. Ham radio built friendships across the Iron Curtain in Morse; CB gave truckers a rolling party line. Static, skip, and the magic of a far station fading in — no stream ever felt like that.

The Spark-Gap Transmitter carries that cultural charge directly: Banned for interference; CW (continuous wave) replaced it.

title: Collecting and Preserving Spark-Gap Transmitter
body:
Cathedral and tombstone cabinets: check for intact grilles and unmolested chassis. Transistor portables (TR-63, TR-1) are hot; working examples cost real money. Hams collect QSL cards and keys. Always replace paper caps and the line filter before powering tube sets — 'all American five' AA5 sets have hot chassis; use an isolation transformer.

For the Spark-Gap Transmitter specifically: The original radio: high-voltage sparks radiating damped waves — broad, buzzy, and illegal by 1930.. Prioritize completeness and originality over shine; a working Spark-Gap Transmitter with honest wear outranks a polished non-runner.

title: Spark-Gap Transmitter Restoration Guide
body:
Recap (electrolytics + paper), check tubes, align IF/RF with a signal generator — don't just 'tweak until loud'. Replace line cords; add fuses. Refinish cabinets sympathetically; keep original knobs. For AA5 sets: isolation transformer, always.

Restoration order for a Spark-Gap Transmitter: 1) document everything photographically before touching it; 2) stabilize (clean, de-corrode, free seized parts); 3) repair before replacing; 4) replace only what is missing or dangerous, marking replacements; 5) test under supervision. Never power an unrestored electrical radio record without a current-limited bring-up.

title: Spark-Gap Transmitter — Superheterodyne planner + LC resonance (Runnable Python)
body:
Computes resonant frequency for tuner LC values, the superhet image frequency problem, and wavelength — the core math of every radio dial.

The program below is real, runnable Python 3. Save it as demo.py and run `python3 demo.py`. It models the core mathematics of the Spark-Gap Transmitter so you can experiment with the parameters yourself.
code:
# Radio math: resonance, superhet images, wavelength (public-domain formulas)
import math

def resonance_lc(l_uh, c_pf):
    l, c = l_uh * 1e-6, c_pf * 1e-12
    f = 1 / (2 * math.pi * math.sqrt(l * c))
    return f

def superhet(station_mhz, if_mhz=10.7, high_side=True):
    lo = station_mhz + if_mhz if high_side else station_mhz - if_mhz
    image = lo + if_mhz if high_side else lo - if_mhz
    return lo, image

# FM tuner: 100 uH coil, what capacitance tunes 88-108 MHz?
for f_mhz in (88, 98, 108):
    f = f_mhz * 1e6
    c = 1 / ((2 * math.pi * f) ** 2 * 100e-6) * 1e12
    print(f"tune {f_mhz} MHz with 100uH -> {c:.1f} pF")

lo, img = superhet(98.5)
print(f"\n98.5 MHz station: LO={lo:.1f} MHz, image at {img:.1f} MHz (must be filtered!)")
print(f"wavelength of 98.5 MHz: {300/98.5:.2f} m ; quarter-wave whip: {300/98.5/4:.2f} m")
